title: Malaysia Talks With US on AI Chip Curbs, Tightens Controls
summary: Malaysia's finance minister confirms compliance discussions with US over new AI chip restrictions affecting Nvidia technology access in Southeast Asia.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Malaysia's government is actively negotiating with US authorities over new AI chip export controls requiring licenses for advanced Nvidia processors.
- The Southeast Asian nation has pledged full compliance and is tightening controls after three entities were blacklisted for alleged chip smuggling.
- CIMB Bank warns Malaysia could lose 0.19 percentage points of GDP growth in 2027 under worst-case disruption scenarios.


Malaysia's government is downplaying the economic impact of sweeping new US restrictions on AI chip technology while simultaneously pledging full compliance with Washington's export controls. Second Finance Minister Amir Hamzah Azizan confirmed that Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry is holding active discussions with US authorities to find common ground on rules that could significantly affect the nation's booming data center industry.


## Official Response to US Chip Restrictions


Officially launched on November 25, 2026, Malaysia's compliance strategy comes in response to a US Commerce Department interim rule released the previous week. The measure requires data center operators in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia to obtain US government licenses before purchasing[advanced AI chips](https://emergent.sh/glossary/ai-chip) from Nvidia and other American manufacturers. The policy aims to prevent China and other US adversaries from accessing offshore computing power built on American-designed processors.


"We will comply with whatever rules are set by the relevant country," Amir told Bloomberg TV, emphasizing that Malaysia expects both sides will reach agreement through ongoing negotiations. The minister stressed that Malaysia had not approved shipments currently being questioned by US authorities and is taking concrete steps to prevent similar incidents.


## Blacklisted Entities and Smuggling Concerns


The US blacklisted several Southeast Asian entities from accessing high-end chip technology over concerns that advanced Nvidia processors are being smuggled to China through the region. While Washington initially identified three Malaysian entities, Kuala Lumpur clarified that only two are actually Malaysian. The government has since instructed data center operators not to host, lease space to, or provide services to any blacklisted firms.


"This is in relation to the Nvidia issue," Amir said. "Effectively we're just tightening up controls." The minister emphasized that Malaysia's hyperscalers are predominantly western-dominated companies using compute capacity for their own internal operations, not exclusively for AI applications but also for cloud services and other workloads.


## Economic Impact and Industry Exposure


CIMB Bank Bhd projects that Malaysia stands to lose the most among Southeast Asian nations under the new restrictions. The bank's worst-case scenario forecasts a 0.19 percentage point reduction in GDP growth for 2027, assuming a six-month disruption to data center operations and postponement of 25% of ongoing construction capacity.


"Malaysia's lead in ASEAN data centre buildout is a double-edge sword," CIMB warned in a November 19 report. "Its dominance in live AI capacity, alongside substantial construction and planned pipeline across all workloads, leaves it exposed to the direct and grey-area regulatory risks." The analysis highlights Malaysia's outsized exposure given its market-leading position in regional data center development.


## Investment Pipeline and Economic Performance


Despite the regulatory headwinds, Malaysia's investment momentum remains strong. The government approved 350.4 billion ringgit ($85 billion) in investments during the first nine months of 2026, a 21% increase year-over-year. Data center and cloud projects accounted for more than one-third of this total at 123.5 billion ringgit, underscoring the sector's importance to Malaysia's economic strategy.


Record-high exports driven by sustained demand for AI-related products helped Malaysia's economy expand 5.5% in the third quarter of 2026, exceeding the government's revised forecast range of 4.8% to 5.3% growth for the full year. Amir expressed confidence that demand fundamentals remain intact despite the new controls. "The reality is compute demand will continue to move on," he said.


## What This Means


Malaysia's diplomatic approach reflects the delicate balance Southeast Asian nations must strike between maintaining access to critical US technology and avoiding secondary sanctions related to China. The government's compliance pledge and control-tightening measures signal recognition that cooperation with Washington is essential for preserving Malaysia's data center industry. However, the CIMB analysis suggests real economic costs if negotiations fail to produce workable licensing frameworks that allow legitimate business operations to continue. The outcome of Malaysia's talks with US authorities will likely set precedents for how other Southeast Asian nations navigate similar chip export restrictions in the months ahead.
